name: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
title: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
answer: Data warehouses and lakehouses store an organisation's analytical history in tables queried with SQL. The major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. This page covers the storage and query layer itself, the AI features vendors have added to it, and the ways analysts and data teams reach both through SQL. It sits alongside the wider AI and SQL field, where the same tables are also read by agents and applications.

sections.body: Data warehouses and lakehouses store an organisation's analytical history in tables queried with SQL. The major platforms now offer AI functions and model serving inside the platform, so data does not have to leave governed storage to be used by a model. This page covers the storage and query layer itself, the AI features vendors have added to it, and the ways analysts and data teams reach both through SQL. It sits alongside the wider AI and SQL field, where the same tables are also read by agents and applications.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A warehouse runs on managed compute over columnar storage, with separate clusters or warehouses sized for each workload. A lakehouse keeps files in cheap object storage, typically Parquet or similar open formats, and puts a table format and a query engine over them so the files behave like tables. Vendors sell these as hosted services, and open engines such as Spark and Trino can query the same files on your own machines. Model endpoints, vector indexes and feature stores are increasingly deployed next to the data rather than in a separate stack.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with ingestion and modelling: raw files and change streams land in staging tables, then get cleaned, joined and shaped into facts and dimensions or wide analytical tables. Analysts and applications query those tables in SQL, and increasingly call AI functions from the same statement, for example to classify text, generate an embedding or score a row with a hosted model. Retrieval patterns add a vector column and a similarity search beside ordinary filters, so a query can mix exact conditions with semantic ones. Pipelines are scheduled or triggered, tested, and versioned like other code, and results are materialised when a query is too slow to run live.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because the data stays in governed storage, existing controls still apply: role based access, row and column level policies, masking, and audit logs of who queried what. Provenance matters when a model writes back into a table, so teams record which model, prompt or feature set produced a value and keep the source rows traceable. Cost and quota controls matter too, since a careless AI function over a large table can consume far more compute than a plain select. Where personal or regulated data is involved, the platform's residency, retention and deletion rules govern the model calls as much as the tables. Nothing here is legal advice, and specific obligations depend on your jurisdiction and sector.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward one governed store that serves both classical analytics and model workloads, with SQL as the common interface. Expect more pushdown of model inference into the query engine, tighter coupling between tables and vector indexes, and catalogues that describe models and features as first class assets. Agent access is the newer pressure: this site currently tracks 2,604 active Model Context Protocol servers, 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses, which suggests assistants will query these systems directly rather than through hand built dashboards. The open question is whether lakehouse formats and warehouse engines converge on one standard or keep competing on performance and governance.
